title: Is personality stable across the lifespan?

readings.title: Source 1: Source 1
readings.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked how consistent people's Big Five trait scores are over long periods.

Participants

1,200 adults in Germany, ages 30 to 60 at the start, followed for 12 years.

Method

Participants completed the same Big Five personality inventory at the start and again 12 years later. For each trait, the researchers correlated each person's first score with their second score (rank-order consistency).

Results

Scores at the two times were strongly positively correlated for every trait, from r=0.62r = 0.62 for agreeableness to r=0.74r = 0.74 for extraversion. People who scored high relative to others at the start usually still scored high 12 years later.

Invented study for practice.

readings.title: Source 2: Source 2
readings.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether average trait levels shift as people move from adolescence into middle age.

Participants

3,000 people in the Netherlands, in five age groups (15, 25, 35, 45 and 55 years old), 600 per group.

Method

Each participant completed a Big Five inventory once. The researchers compared the mean conscientiousness score (scale 1 to 5) across the age groups.

Results

Mean conscientiousness rose from 3.0 at age 15 to 3.6 at age 25, 3.8 at age 35, 3.9 at age 45 and 4.0 at age 55. Older groups also scored somewhat higher on agreeableness and lower on neuroticism.

Invented study for practice.

readings.title: Source 3: Source 3
readings.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether a major new social role, a first full-time job, goes with changes in conscientiousness.

Participants

400 young adults in Australia, ages 20 to 24, followed for four years.

Method

Participants completed a Big Five inventory every year. The researchers compared the change in conscientiousness (scale 1 to 5) between those who began a first full-time job during the study and those who did not.

Results

Conscientiousness rose by a mean of 0.4 points in those who started a full-time job and by 0.1 points in those who did not.

Invented study for practice.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Propose a specific and defensible claim based in psychological science that responds to the question: is personality stable across the lifespan?

rubric.point: States a defensible claim that answers the question (not a question, a topic sentence or a summary of one source).
accept: traits are fairly stable in how people rank relative to others, but average levels change with age
personality is mostly stable across adulthood
personality changes across the lifespan, especially from adolescence to middle age

parts.sample: Personality traits are fairly stable across adulthood in how people compare with one another, but they still change in predictable ways as people age and take on new roles.

parts.label: B(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using at least one piece of specific and relevant evidence from one of the sources.

rubric.point: Gives a specific, accurate result from one source and cites the source.
accept: Source 1: scores 12 years apart correlated from 0.62 to 0.74 for every trait
Source 2: mean conscientiousness rose from 3.0 at age 15 to 4.0 at age 55

parts.sample: According to Source 1, adults' Big Five scores at the start and 12 years later were strongly positively correlated for every trait, from 0.62 for agreeableness to 0.74 for extraversion (Source 1).

parts.label: B(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from B(i) supports your claim using a psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding learned in AP® Psychology.

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
accept: strong correlations mean people who were high relative to others stayed high, so their relative standing was stable

rubric.point: Applies a relevant psychology concept, not a restricted term, linked to the evidence and the claim.
accept: trait theory: traits are stable tendencies, which fits people keeping their rank on the Big Five
the Big Five traits are partly heritable, which helps explain why rank order stays consistent
temperament: early, partly inborn tendencies carry forward into adult traits, which keeps people's rank similar

parts.sample: This supports the claim because a strong positive correlation means that the people who were most extraverted, for example, at the start were still among the most extraverted 12 years later. That fits trait theory, which describes the Big Five traits as stable tendencies that show across situations and time. Because traits like these are partly heritable, it makes sense that people keep a similar rank relative to others even as their lives change.

parts.label: C(i)
parts.prompt: Support your claim using a different piece of specific and relevant evidence from another source.

rubric.point: Gives a specific, accurate result from a different source than B(i), and cites it.
accept: Source 3: conscientiousness rose 0.4 points in those who started a full-time job versus 0.1 in those who did not
Source 2: mean conscientiousness rose from 3.0 at 15 to 4.0 at 55

parts.sample: In Source 3, young adults who started their first full-time job increased in conscientiousness by a mean of 0.4 points over four years, compared with 0.1 points for those who did not start one (Source 3).

parts.label: C(ii)
parts.prompt: Explain how the evidence from C(i) supports your claim using a different psychological perspective, theory, concept or research finding than the one used in B(ii).

rubric.point: Explains how the evidence supports the claim.
accept: traits still changed in a predictable direction when people took on a new role, so personality is not fixed

rubric.point: Applies a different relevant concept than in B(ii), not a restricted term, linked to the evidence and the claim.
accept: reciprocal determinism: a new work environment and new behavior feed back on the person's traits
social role: the expectations of a worker's role push behavior toward being more organized and reliable
self-efficacy: success at work builds confidence that supports more careful, planned behavior

parts.sample: This supports the claim that traits change in predictable ways, because starting a demanding new role was followed by a larger rise in conscientiousness. Reciprocal determinism explains why: the new work environment required organized, reliable behavior, and practicing that behavior day after day fed back on the person, so their conscientiousness grew. So even though people keep a similar rank, the settings and roles they enter can still shift their traits.
